description.narrative:
Kenyas regering (GoK) vill förbättra leveransen av lokalt ledda åtgärder för klimatresiliens för att öka samhällens motståndskraft mot klimatförändringar och andra risker. Den föreslagna insatsen heter Financing Locally-Led Climate Action (FLLoCA) som syftar till att bidra till en utvecklingsväg med låga koldioxidutsläpp och förbättrad klimatresiliens för att nå Vision 2030 (Kenyas utvecklingsplan) och därefter.
FLLoCA-programmet kommer att implementeras som ett hybridprogram med två komponenter; Performance for Results, PforR och Investment Project Financing, IPF. IPF-komponenten kommer att stödja kapaciteten för hantering av klimatrisker på nationell nivå, medan PforR-komponenten kommer att stödja GoKs program för att adressera klimatförändringar på länsnivå genom att finansiera åtgärder för klimatresiliens och öka Council of governors (CG) kapacitet att hantera klimatrisker.
Insatsen är en fortsättning av av den just avslutade (2013–2020) Adaconsortium insatsen (insatssnummer 11085) implementerad av International Institute for Environment and Development (IIED) samt finansierad av Sida och Storbritanniens avdelning för internationell utveckling (tidigare DFID). Adaconsortium stödde 5 län (Garissa, Isiolo, Kitui, Makueni och Wajir) för att genomföra den nationella handlingsplanen för klimatförändringar (NCCAP) genom County Climate Change Fund (CCCF). Den nya fasen kommer att genomföras på nationell skala (med avtalspartnern Världsbanken) och kopplar åtgärder på lokal nivå till samordning och planering på nationell nivå.
Världsbanken har lämnat in ett förslag med en total budget på 173,2 miljoner USD för hela FLLoCA-programmet (2021-2026), som ska ligga under Världsbankens Social Sustainability for All (SSI4ALL) Trust Fund. I detta belopp är 87% (150mUSD) från Världsbanken som kredit till den kenyanska regeringen, 5% (9 mUSD) från Danmarks regering som ett bidrag och 8% (14,2 mUSD motsvarande 120 mkr) från Sida.
Covid-19-pandemin har identifierats som en av de stora riskerna som potentiellt hot mot genomförandet av insatsens mål och som ambassaden måste övervaka och anpassa vid behov.

The Government of Kenya (GoK) is looking to enhance the delivery of locally-led climate resilience actions in order to increase communities’ resilience to climate change and other hazards. The proposed Contribution is titled Financing Locally-Led Climate Action (FLLoCA) which aims to contribute to a low carbon development pathway with enhanced climate resilience towards the attainment of Vision 2030 (Kenya's development blueprint) and beyond.
The FLLoCA program will be implemented as a hybrid Program for Results (PforR) and Investment Project Financing (IPF). The IPF component will support climate risk management capacities at the national level while the PforR component will support the GoK’s program to address climate change at the county level by financing climate resilience actions and increasing County Government's (CGs’) climate risk management capacities.
The Contribution is a follow up of the just concluded (2013-2020) Sida and United Kingdom Department for International Development (formerly DFID) support to International Institute for Environment and Development (IIED)/Adaconsortium (Contribution number 11085). The Adaconsortium supported 5 Counties (Garissa, Isiolo, Kitui, Makueni, and Wajir) to implement the National Climate Change Action Plan (NCCAP) through the County Climate Change Fund (CCCF). This phase will be national in scale (with the agreement partner being the World Bank), linking local level action to national level coordination and planning.
WBG has submitted a proposal with a total budget of 173.2USDM for the entire FLLoCA Programme (2021-2026), which shall be under WB's Social Sustainability for All (SSI4ALL) Trust Fund. With this figure, 87% (150MUSD) is from WBG as credit to the Kenyan Government, 5% (9MUSD) from Government of Denmark as a grant and 8% (14.2MUSD equivalent to 120MSEK) from Sida.
Covid-19 pandemic has been identified among the major risks with potential threat towards realization of the Contribution's objective which Sida has to monitor and adapt where necessary.

The program seeks to deliver locally-led climate resilience actions and strengthening county and national governments capacity to manage climate risk with the long-term aim of increasing local-level resilience to climate change and other hazards. The Performance for Results (PforR) component finances county-level performance grants that will result in a portfolio of climate resilience actions/investments addressing communities priorities and an increased capacity of County Governments (CGs) to manage climate risk.
The Investment Project Financing (IPF) component finances national-level capacity building actions and operationalize the Inter-Agency Climate Finance Technical Advisory Committee (CF-TAC) - comprising representatives from relevant line ministries, the Chairperson of the Council of Governors (CoG), and representatives from the private sector, civil society, vulnerable and marginalized groups, academia, and development partners, which is the official cross-sectoral climate coordination entity, resulting in an increased capacity of the national government to manage climate risk.
The contribution has identified critical assumptions necessary in order to achieve objectives. These include the ability of counties to meet performance conditions to allow them to access grant resources; effective participatory processes and use of climate risk mapping results to select climate resilience investments; national entities willingness to work together; and effective implementation of selected climate resilience investments.

description.narrative:
Results Area 1: Strengthening County Institutional Capacity for Locally Led Climate Action In its fourth year of implementation, the Financing Locally Led Climate Action (FLLoCA) programme has made substantial progress in strengthening county level institutional capacity for climate governance and resilience planning. Through three annual County Climate Institutional Support (CCIS) grant cycles, totaling US$13.4 million, the programme has supported all 47 counties to establish the policy, institutional, and financial systems necessary for sustained climate action. As a result, all 47 counties have enacted Climate Change Acts, embedding climate governance structures and climate financing mechanisms within county systems. In addition, 44 counties have allocated at least 1.5 percent of their development budgets to County Climate Change Funds (CCCFs), while 45 counties have established and maintained fully staffed Climate Change Units. These achievements have enhanced the predictability, coordination, and accessibility of climate finance at the local level, creating a stronger foundation for climate responsive development. At the community level, the programme has strengthened participatory and inclusive climate planning through the establishment and operationalization of 1,335 Ward Climate Change Planning Committees and 1,580 Project Management Committees. These structures continue to play a critical role in identifying, prioritizing, and overseeing climate resilient investments that respond to local needs and vulnerabilities. Continuous technical support from national institutions has further strengthened institutional capacity at both county and community levels, ensuring that climate investments are informed by climate risk assessments and evidence based decision making processes. The effectiveness of these interventions is reflected in county performance results, with average scores increasing from 61 percent in the first Annual Performance Assessment to 87 percent in the second assessment. This significant improvement demonstrates the Programs success in institutionalizing climate governance systems and enhancing counties capacity to deliver locally led climate action.
Results Area 2: Delivery of Locally Led Climate Resilience Investments FLLoCA has enabled counties to translate climate policy commitments into tangible investments that strengthen community resilience and adaptive capacity. Under the first cycle of the County Climate Resilient Investment (CCRI) Grants, counties identified 2,245 climate related sub projects across priority sectors. To date, 1,571 investments have been implemented, including 1,014 completed projects and 466 ongoing initiatives across 45 counties. The programme has reached approximately 2.5 million direct and indirect beneficiaries, of whom 54 percent are women, across 1,238 wards. These investments are already delivering important social and economic benefits, particularly for vulnerable groups. Beneficiaries include approximately 29,000 women, 37,000 youth, and 2,496 persons with disabilities, demonstrating the Programs commitment to inclusive and equitable climate action. Investment patterns reflect county priorities and climate resilience needs, with resources concentrated in water (46 percent), environment and natural resource management (25 percent), agriculture (22 percent), and other sectors (7 percent). This portfolio underscores the programme's strong focus on climate adaptation and community resilience building. Despite this progress, implementation has faced a number of challenges that have affected the pace and efficiency of delivery. Key constraints include delays in procurement and fund disbursement processes, community and stakeholder engagement challenges, climatic and environmental disruptions, institutional capacity limitations, and weaknesses in project reporting and documentation. These factors have contributed to implementation delays and coordination challenges at both county and community levels. To address these constraints and enhance future performance, the programme has identified several corrective measures. These include improving the alignment of procurement and fund disbursement processes with implementation timelines strengthening community sensitization, stakeholder engagement, and grievance redress mechanisms enhancing climate responsive planning and environmental screening building institutional capacity and inter agency coordination, with stronger integration of gender and youth considerations and investing in more robust, participatory, and digitally enabled Monitoring, Evaluation, and Learning (MEL) systems. These actions are expected to improve implementation efficiency, accountability, and the sustainability of climate resilience outcomes in subsequent investment cycles.
